cues.text: The Investiture Controversy
For half a century, popes and Holy Roman Emperors had contested who held the right to invest bishops and abbots with the ring and staff symbolizing their office.
The struggle pitted spiritual and temporal authority against one another at the highest level and had already produced Emperor Henry IV’s dramatic penance before Pope Gregory VII at Canossa in 1077.
There, the excommunicated emperor reportedly stood barefoot in the snow for three days seeking absolution.

The conflict dragged on under Henry's son, Henry V , and successive popes, disrupting church governance across the empire for a generation, leaving bishoprics vacant or filled by rival claimants for years at a stretch.
A resolution finally came through the diplomacy of Pope Callistus II , elected in 1119 with a reputation as a skilled negotiator from his years as Archbishop of Vienne.
He opened direct talks with Henry V. The two sides met at Worms in September 1122 and produced the Concordat of Worms , the first formal treaty ever signed between pope and emperor.
It distinguished a bishop’s spiritual investiture, reserved to the Church, from the grant of his temporal fiefs and regalia, retained by the emperor.
Confirming the Concordat at Rome
So significant was this settlement that contemporaries dated a new era from it.

To give the agreement the fullest possible solemnity, Callistus II summoned a general council to Rome, convoked in December 1122 and opened at the Lateran in March 1123 — the first ecumenical council ever held in Western Europe.
Some three hundred bishops and more than six hundred abbots gathered under the pope's personal presidency, an extraordinarily large assembly for its time.

Both original copies ( instrumenta ) of the Concordat of Worms were solemnly read aloud and formally ratified by the council, giving the settlement the weight of a universal Church decision rather than a mere bilateral agreement.
Disciplinary Canons
Beyond ratifying the Concordat, the council issued twenty-two disciplinary canons addressing abuses that had multiplied during decades of disputed episcopal appointments.

Among the most significant were these measures: Forbidding priests, deacons, subdeacons, and monks to marry or keep concubines, declaring such marriages null Voiding the ordinations performed by the antipope Burdinus (Gregory VIII) after his condemnation Renewing protections for crusaders' families and property while they were away on campaign Reaffirming penalties against simony, the buying and selling of church offices Many of these canons reinforced decrees from earlier regional reform councils, giving them now the authority of a universal assembly.
Ending Imperial Interference
Beyond its immediate disciplinary content, the council's deeper achievement was constitutional: it tacitly ended the emperors' long-claimed right to interfere directly in papal elections.
It reestablished the freedom of episcopal and abbatial elections from lay control, and firmly separated spiritual authority from purely temporal grants of land and office.
The council insisted that spiritual authority could emanate only from the Church.

This settlement did not eliminate all future friction between empire and papacy — later centuries would see fresh conflicts — but it closed the specific, acute crisis of lay investiture that had convulsed Church governance since the mid-eleventh century.
Legacy
First Lateran was the first ecumenical council held in the West and the first since the definitive break between Rome and Constantinople in 1054.

It also marked a turning point in the character of general councils themselves: from this point on, the ecumenical councils recognized by the Catholic Church would be Western, papally convoked assemblies rather than the emperor-summoned gatherings of the patristic era.
No council would meet again in the East with Rome's participation.
Its settlement of the investiture question established a template — the careful separation of spiritual and temporal authority.
This template would shape Church-state relations across Europe for centuries afterward.
Fresh disputes between popes and emperors, and later between popes and national monarchs, would continue to erupt in new forms for the rest of the medieval period.
